justice: The street space is dominated by a wide unmarked carriageway, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible on either side, indicating poor spatial allocation for non-motorized users.
Construction debris and dumped waste occupy the left roadside, and stacked industrial materials occupy the right edge, reducing fair access to the public realm for all users.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free pedestrian facilities are visible, which weakens accessibility in the shared street environment.
safety: A black car, a parked white car, a truck, and a motorcyclist all use the same dusty, unmarked roadway, increasing conflict risk because there is no visible lane separation.
The road surface appears unpaved or heavily dust-covered and uneven, which can reduce tire grip and increase stopping distance for vehicles and bicycles.
Roadside debris on the left and stacked panels/materials on the right create edge hazards and may narrow the usable space for passing road users.
livability: The visible environment is primarily industrial/storage-oriented, with corrugated sheds on the right and material stacks rather than active public-facing uses.
Open dumping and scattered rubble on the left side lower environmental quality and make the street less suitable for everyday social life.
There are no visible benches, storefronts, public gathering spaces, or pedestrian amenities that would support daily community interaction.
sustainability: Only a few trees are visible in the middle distance, while most of the corridor lacks meaningful green infrastructure or continuous planting.
The street design shows no visible bike lane, transit stop, or pedestrian infrastructure that would encourage low-carbon travel choices.
The dusty bare road surface and unmanaged roadside waste suggest weak environmental management and no evident stormwater or ecological design features.
aesthetics: Piles of garbage and rubble on the left side create strong visual disorder and reduce perceived street quality.
Industrial sheds, exposed stacks of dark construction materials, and an unpaved dusty roadway give the corridor a harsh and utilitarian appearance.
The few trees and distant residential buildings provide limited visual relief, but they are not enough to offset the overall cluttered streetscape.
comfort: Tree shade is minimal and discontinuous, and the broad exposed roadway offers little thermal protection under the clear sky.
There is no visible sidewalk, seating, or paved pedestrian refuge, reducing physical comfort for anyone moving along the corridor on foot.
The presence of industrial storage, debris, and mixed vehicle movement can create psychological discomfort due to disorder and uncertainty about safe movement space.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, forcing pedestrians to share space directly with cars, trucks, and motorcycles on the main roadway.
The road edge is obstructed by dumped waste on the left and stacked materials on the right, leaving little clearly walkable margin.
There are no marked crossings, curb protections, pedestrian signs, or shading elements that would support safe and attractive walking.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, shoulder, or pavement marking to organize cycling space on the corridor.
Cyclists would need to ride in the same dusty roadway as cars, trucks, and motorcycles, increasing exposure to traffic conflicts.
The rough dirt-like surface and roadside obstacles from debris and stored materials would make cycling less stable and less comfortable.
